title: Hold up his arms (Exodus 17:8–13)
hookLine: Moses' arms tire on the hill, and Aaron and Hur hold them up

lines: ARMS UP: TEN SECONDS, A MINUTE.
UP THE HILL, STAFF IN HAND.
cards: Try this, if you can. Raise both arms over your head and hold them there. Ten seconds is easy.
Thirty, your shoulders start to burn. A minute, and they shake. Now imagine holding them up until sunset.
At a place called Rephidim, a people called Amalek attack Israel. A later book says they struck at the stragglers, the tired and weak at the back.
Moses sends a man named Joshua to choose fighters and lead them, and climbs a hill with the staff of God in his hand, and two companions: his brother Aaron, and a man named Hur.

teach.b: Then a strange battle report, in the King James translation: "when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed." The fight in the valley follows Moses's arms on the hill.
What did the raised hands mean? The text doesn't explain. It only shows.
The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching, asks it directly: did Moses's hands make the war or break it? Its answer: when Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to God, they prevailed.
Christian readers have seen prayer in it too. And Moses gets tired.

"But Moses' hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun."
First a stone, so he can sit. No shame in sitting.
Then one on each side, holding up an arm. They don't take the staff. They don't do his job.
They just hold up what he can't hold alone anymore. Nobody tells Moses to be stronger. Heavy is allowed.
Christians have read this as a picture of praying for one another and carrying each other, and some churches speak of holding up their pastors' arms. Joshua wins the battle below.

teach.h: HIS HANDS WERE STEADY UNTIL THE GOING DOWN OF THE SUN.
teach.b: But the picture that lasts is up on the hill: three people, one stone, and arms that stay up until sunset.

how: Some Christians use the picture of Aaron and Hur holding up Moses's hands when they pray for their pastors, missionaries and one another, and some churches form prayer teams named for it.

games.q: you're Aaron, on the hill beside your brother. the battle turns whenever his arms drop, and now they're shaking. what do you do?
o: take the staff and hold it up yourself.
find him a stone to sit on, and hold up one of his arms.

games.why: they put a stone under him, and Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on each side, and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.

practice: Let your arms rest in your lap, and think of someone whose arms are heavy right now: a parent of small children, a caregiver, a nurse, a friend carrying more than their share.
Picture yourself on one side of them, holding up an arm, and let one real way to help come to mind, a meal, a ride, an hour of your time. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
